title: Christ accepts the temple and ancient prophets restore keys
setting: One week after the dedication, on Easter Sunday, 3 April 1836, the Saints met in the Kirtland temple. After the sacrament, Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery withdrew behind lowered veils at the pulpit to pray in silence. Warren A. Cowdery recorded their account in Joseph’s journal in the third person. Willard Richards later recast it in the first person, and it entered the Doctrine and Covenants in 1876.
summary: The account says the veil was taken from the minds of Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery. They report seeing the Lord standing on the pulpit, with eyes like fire and a voice like rushing waters. He declares their sins forgiven and says he has accepted the house. He promises to appear there if his people keep it holy, and says its fame will spread. Then Moses appears and commits the keys of gathering Israel and leading the ten tribes. Elias commits the dispensation of the gospel of Abraham. Elijah appears last, saying the time Malachi spoke of has fully come. He commits keys tied to turning the hearts of fathers and children to each other.

contextNote.title: An answer to the dedicatory prayer
contextNote.text: One week earlier, the dedicatory prayer had asked God to accept the house. Verse 7 reports the answer in direct speech: “I have accepted this house”. The voice adds “my name shall be here” and promises to appear in mercy. Verse 8 sets a condition: the people must keep the commandments and not pollute it. The keys in verses 11–16 come only after this acceptance. In this account, acceptance means the house becomes a place where the Lord says he will show himself.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 109–110 connects these visions to temple blessings. What keys are named in verses 11–16, and what work does each one point to?
reviewNote: Read all 16 verses. Official heading gives the Kirtland temple, Easter Sunday 3 April 1836, Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery praying behind dropped veils. JSP introduction read for Warren A. Cowdery’s third-person journal entry, Willard Richards’s first-person revision by 1843, and 1876 canonization. No contemporary record by Joseph or Oliver themselves survives beyond the journal entry.
